blockMcqs.question: What combination does good design aim for?
options: High coupling, high cohesion
Low coupling, high cohesion
High coupling, low cohesion
Low coupling, low cohesion
blockMcqs.explanation: Low coupling limits how far a change spreads; high cohesion keeps each module focused on one job.

blockMcqs.question: What does loose coupling mean in practice?
options: A class builds its dependency's concrete class
A class depends only on a stable interface
A class has no dependencies at all
A class shares private fields directly
blockMcqs.explanation: Loose coupling means depending on a contract (interface), not on another class's implementation details.

blockMcqs.question: Under tight coupling, what happens when you swap an implementation?
options: Nothing changes anywhere
It drops in with no edits
The dependent class needs edits too
Only tests need updates
blockMcqs.explanation: Tight coupling means the dependent class knows the concrete class, so swapping it forces changes there too.

blockMcqs.question: High cohesion in a class means what?
options: It has many unrelated responsibilities
It depends on many other classes
All its parts serve one clear purpose
It has no public methods
blockMcqs.explanation: High cohesion means every method and field in the class works toward the same single purpose.

blockMcqs.question: What's a warning sign of low cohesion?
options: The class has one obvious reason to change
The class name matches its single job
The class changes for several unrelated reasons
The class has no dependencies
blockMcqs.explanation: A class touched for many unrelated reasons is mixing responsibilities, which is the hallmark of low cohesion.

blockMcqs.question: How does loose coupling help testing?
options: It removes the need for tests
It lets a mock stand in for the real dependency
It forces every test to hit the database
It hides bugs from test coverage
blockMcqs.explanation: Depending on an interface means a test can substitute a mock or fake without touching the class under test.

blockMcqs.question: Which practice most directly lowers coupling?
options: Adding more public fields
Constructing dependencies inside the class
Injecting a dependency via its interface
Merging several classes into one
blockMcqs.explanation: Dependency injection against an interface removes the class's need to know a concrete implementation.

blockMcqs.question: In the pseudocode, what changed 'after'?
options: OrderService now sends emails via SMTP directly
OrderService depends on a Notifier interface
OrderService no longer saves the order
OrderService lost its constructor
blockMcqs.explanation: The class now holds a Notifier interface field, injected via the constructor, instead of building SmtpEmailSender itself.

blockMcqs.question: Which SOLID principle maps most directly to low coupling?
options: Single responsibility
Dependency inversion
Liskov substitution
Interface segregation
blockMcqs.explanation: Dependency inversion — depend on abstractions, not concretions — is the core recipe behind low coupling.

blockMcqs.question: Why is 'zero coupling' a flawed goal?
options: It is always achievable with enough interfaces
Modules must collaborate, so some contact is required
It guarantees high cohesion automatically
It eliminates the need for testing
blockMcqs.explanation: Modules need to interact to do useful work; the real goal is thin, stable contracts, not total isolation.
